vignette:
Amir describes his life before as being lived in color. For thirty years, he and his wife, Layla, had built a world rich with texture. He was the performer, the one who lived for the stage lights and the applause, and she was his anchor, his first audience. She would run lines with him in their small, sun-filled kitchen, her gentle critiques always sharpening his performance. He remembers the scent of cardamom and mint tea that always seemed to hang in the air around her. He was a working actor, never a star, but he found deep satisfaction in the craft, a pride that was mirrored in her eyes after every performance. The life they had was not grand, but it was vibrant and it was theirs.

The color began to drain from the world two years ago on a Tuesday. They were in the living room, watching an old film, and he had just gotten up to get them both more tea. He heard a sound—not a cry, but a sharp, confused gasp, followed by the soft thud of her body slumping from the armchair to the floor. The next few hours are a chaotic, fragmented reel that plays in his mind without his permission. The slick feel of the phone as he fumbled to dial for an ambulance. The strange, distorted sound of his own voice, begging her to wake up. The paramedics’ calm, procedural movements, which felt like a violent intrusion. The sterile, antiseptic smell of the hospital corridor that replaced the familiar scent of their home. He remembers sitting in a plastic chair, staring at the linoleum floor, while the doctor explained the severity of the hemorrhagic stroke. He remembers nodding, but not comprehending. Layla never regained consciousness. She was gone three days later.

Now, at fifty-two, Amir lives in a world of grayscale. The apartment is silent, meticulously clean, and ordered in a way Layla, with her creative clutter, would have found amusing. He avoids the kitchen for as long as he can each morning. He makes his coffee in the living room with an electric kettle. He tells himself it’s more efficient, but he knows it’s because the spot on the floor where she fell feels permanently cold to him.

His work, once his sanctuary, has become a minefield. Last month, during a rehearsal for a small stage play, a fellow actor dropped a wooden prop, and the sharp crack against the stage floor sent a jolt through Amir’s body. He was instantly back in his living room, hearing the thud of her fall. He flinched so violently that he stumbled backward, snapping at the startled stagehand with a rage that shocked them both. He is constantly on edge, scanning the faces of his castmates for any flicker of pity or concern, which he interprets as a threat. Sleep offers little respite, often interrupted by vivid nightmares of hospital machinery and the rhythmic, unnatural sound of the ventilator.

He still works, because the structure is the only thing keeping him afloat. He is a master of wearing a mask; his trade has trained him for it. On the outside, he is the consummate professional—lines memorized, character choices deliberate. But inside, he feels like a fraud. He feels a profound detachment from his own life, as if he is watching a character named Amir go through the motions. He finds himself forgetting lines mid-scene, his mind suddenly snagged on an intrusive image of Layla’s hand lying limp on their rug. The joy he once found in embodying another person is gone. Now, he just feels hollow, using the craft not to reveal emotion, but to contain the terrifying emptiness that has taken its place. Friends from the theater community try to reach out, but he keeps them at a distance. He knows they mean well, but their presence only serves to highlight the one presence that is so deafeningly absent.
